# accessibility-audit

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** WCAG 2.2, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ ; axe-core, Deque — https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core
- **Depends on:** wcag (the audit evaluates against its fixed target)
- **Feeds into:** accessibility-testing, keyboard-accessibility, screen-readers, accessibility-law

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** A build, redesign, or release needs an evidence-producing evaluation against WCAG 2.2 AA — before launch, before a procurement claim, or after remediation to verify fixes.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running a quick in-development check (that is accessibility-testing in CI), producing the legal jurisdiction map (accessibility-law), or fixing individual defects (the owning skill, e.g. keyboard-accessibility, does the fix; the audit only finds and records).

## Rules

1. **AC-001 — Fix the scope and target in writing before testing.** The audit plan names the pages, complete processes, and components in scope and states the target as "WCAG 2.2 Level AA" (or the older version a contract or law pins — EAA/EN 301 549 pins 2.1 AA, Section 508 pins 2.0 AA). An audit with no written scope evaluates nothing in particular.
2. **AC-002 — Automated tools are one pass, never the audit.** Automated scanning (axe-core) evaluates only a subset of success criteria. Every audit runs the automated pass AND the manual passes in AC-003; a report based on a tool run alone must state in its own text that it is incomplete.
3. **AC-003 — Every audit includes four passes.** (1) Automated scan over the full scope; (2) keyboard-only walk of every primary process; (3) a smoke test in at least one real screen reader on the primary journeys; (4) visual checks: contrast measurement on rendered colors, 200% zoom, 400% reflow, and focus-visibility observation. Record which pass covered which criteria.
4. **AC-004 — Audit complete processes, not isolated pages.** Scope is defined as user processes (register → verify email → first task; browse → cart → checkout). Conformance is per complete process: a checkout whose step 3 fails is not conformant even if steps 1–2 pass.
5. **AC-005 — Every finding cites a success criterion.** Each finding names the WCAG criterion number it fails (e.g. 1.4.3, 2.4.7, 4.1.2), the page or process step, exact reproduction steps, and a screenshot or recording. A finding worded only as "accessibility issue" is returned for rework.
6. **AC-006 — Severity ranks by user impact, not tool order.** Severity is set by whether the defect blocks, degrades, or merely inconveniences task completion for an affected user group — never by the order or default severity the scanning tool printed.
7. **AC-007 — Report per-criterion conformance, not a verdict.** The report rates each in-scope criterion "supports / partially supports / does not support" (VPAT-style), with the method used per criterion. The word "accessible" never appears as a blanket claim about a page, process, or product.
8. **AC-008 — State the technical result; never a legal conclusion.** Reports state standard, version, level, scope, and date. They never state "ADA compliant" or "legally accessible"; legal applicability is flagged for accessibility-law/D14 to confirm.
9. **AC-009 — Date and version every report; re-audit after fixes.** Conformance decays with every release. Each report carries its date and the build/commit audited; fixed findings are verified by re-running the failing pass, and the re-audit result is appended, not overwritten.
10. **AC-010 — Third-party components are in scope.** Payment widgets, chat embeds, cookie banners, and video players are audited like first-party code (focus order, focus obscured under 2.4.11, iframe titles). "The vendor's widget" is recorded as a finding with the vendor named, never as an exemption.
11. **AC-011 — Triage before sign-off.** Every finding enters a findings register with severity and an owner; sign-off requires zero un-triaged critical findings. Untested scope (e.g. a screen-reader/browser combination not run) is listed as residual risk in the report, not silently omitted.
12. **AC-012 — Method transparency.** The report's method section lists, per pass: tool and version, browser, assistive technology and version, viewport/zoom settings, and the criteria that pass could and could not evaluate — so a reader can see exactly what the evidence does and does not cover.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-001 — Scan-only audit reported as conformance.** Banned: running axe-core (or any automated scanner) and reporting the product "accessible" or "WCAG compliant" from its output alone. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: run all four passes in AC-003 and report per-criterion results under AC-007, naming which criteria each pass covered. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-002 — Findings without a criterion.** Banned: audit findings phrased as "accessibility issue", "not accessible", or "needs improvement" with no WCAG success-criterion number, reproduction steps, or evidence. Defeats: DET-UX-006. Instead: "Checkout step 3 — fails WCAG 1.4.3: placeholder text #9a9a9a on #ffffff (2.6:1) on card-number field; reproduce by loading /checkout/payment; screenshot attached." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-003 — Accessibility overlay offered as the fix.** Banned: installing a third-party "accessibility overlay" widget and closing audit findings against it instead of fixing the underlying code. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: fix the code — give every field a persistent programmatic label — and re-audit the failing pass. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-004 — Clickable divs accepted as controls.** Banned: passing a page whose interactive elements are clickable `<div>`/`<span>` elements with no role, accessible name, or keyboard path, because they "work with a mouse". Defeats: DET-UX-016. Instead: record a 4.1.2/2.1.1 finding with reproduction via the keyboard walk; the fix is a native `<button>` or a full APG-pattern widget. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-005 — Legal verdict in a technical report.** Banned: stating "ADA compliant", "EAA compliant", or "legally accessible" anywhere in an audit deliverable. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: state "Evaluated against WCAG 2.2 Level AA on 2026-11-21; scope and per-criterion results below; legal applicability to be confirmed by D14." Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-001 — Automated scan archived.** Verifies: AC-002, AC-003. Check: run `npx @axe-core/cli <each in-scope URL> --save audit/axe-<date>.json` (or the project's axe-core CI job) over every page and process step in the written scope. Where the axe-core CLI cannot be installed or run, the fallback route is this skill's manual gates G-AC-002 (keyboard walk) and G-AC-004 (criterion checklist) performed and recorded in full, with the substitution recorded in progress.md; the automated run remains required wherever the tooling is available. Pass: a dated report file exists for 100% of in-scope URLs and every violation is entered in the findings register. Fail: block sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-002 — Keyboard walk completed.** Verifies: AC-003, AC-004. Check: manual pass — complete each primary process keyboard-only (Tab/Shift+Tab/Enter/Space/arrow keys/Esc), logging every trap, invisible focus stop, and lost-focus event against its criterion. Agent-evidence form: a scripted keyboard-only traversal (e.g. Playwright driving the same key sequences) that logs the same trap, invisible-stop, and lost-focus findings against their criteria satisfies this gate's evidence, with the traversal script and its log recorded in progress.md; where no scripted traversal can run, this gate is **human-required** and blocks autonomous sign-off until the human walk is recorded. Pass: a completed keyboard-walk checklist exists for every primary process, with findings registered. Fail: block sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-003 — Screen-reader smoke test completed.** Verifies: AC-003, AC-004. Check: manual pass — run the primary journeys in at least one real screen reader (e.g. NVDA + Chrome or VoiceOver + Safari), navigating by headings, landmarks, and form controls; verify accessible names, roles, and live-region announcements. **Human-required:** the evidence is a human listening to real assistive technology; no automated or agent-produced substitute satisfies this gate, and autonomous sign-off is blocked until the human test is recorded. Agent-evidence form (interim evidence only — it prepares and de-risks the human test but never replaces it): the agent records an accessibility-tree audit of each primary journey (accessible names, roles, landmarks, and live regions present and correctly ordered) plus the G-AC-002 keyboard evidence in progress.md, marks this gate human-required, and records a human-evidence waiver request naming the human test still owed. Pass: a dated smoke-test record names the AT/browser versions used and lists pass/fail per journey. Fail: block sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-004 — Criterion checklist complete.** Verifies: AC-005, AC-007, AC-012. Check: open the audit checklist artifact; confirm every in-scope WCAG 2.2 A/AA criterion is marked pass / fail / not-applicable and that each mark names the method (automated, keyboard, screen reader, visual) that produced it. Pass: zero unmarked in-scope criteria. Fail: block sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-005 — Zero un-triaged criticals.** Verifies: AC-006, AC-011. Check: query the findings register for severity = critical AND status = un-triaged. Pass: count is zero, and every critical has an owner and a criterion citation. Fail: block sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- A scan is one pass of four — never the audit.
- No criterion number, no finding.
- Audit processes end to end, not pages.
- Report per criterion: supports, partially, does not.
- Technical result only — legal verdicts belong to D14.

## Checklist

- [ ] Written scope names pages, complete processes, components, and the WCAG version/level target (AC-001).
- [ ] All four passes ran: automated scan, keyboard walk (or its scripted agent-evidence form, G-AC-002), screen-reader smoke test (human-required, G-AC-003), visual checks (AC-003).
- [ ] Every finding cites a success criterion, reproduction steps, and evidence (AC-005).
- [ ] Severities are ranked by user impact, and zero criticals are un-triaged (AC-006, G-AC-005).
- [ ] Report rates conformance per criterion and states method and residual risk (AC-007, AC-011, AC-012).
- [ ] Report contains no legal verdict and no blanket "accessible" claim (AC-008).
- [ ] Report is dated and versioned against the audited build (AC-009).

# accessibility-law

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) summary, EUR-Lex — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=legissum%3A4403933 ; Revised 508 Standards, US Access Board — https://www.access-board.gov/ict/ ; WCAG 2.2, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- **Depends on:** accessibility-audit (its dated per-criterion results are the evidence every statement and map entry rests on), wcag (the conformance target)
- **Feeds into:** legal-documents, compliance-audit (D14 confirms legal applicability and owns the legal determinations)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** A project needs its accessibility obligations mapped before launch, before entering a new market or sector, before bidding on public procurement, or when an accessibility statement or ACR/VPAT must be produced — the output is a recorded technical target: which instrument, which pinned WCAG version and level, which conformance artifact.
- **Do NOT use when:** Giving legal advice or deciding whether a law applies (that is D14/counsel — this skill escalates those questions), running the technical evaluation itself (accessibility-audit), or fixing defects (the owning D13 skill).

## Rules

1. **AC-061 — Map jurisdictions before launch.** Before launch, produce a jurisdiction map in the project's legal file set: for each market served, record the jurisdiction, the sector, the customer type (consumer, business, public procurement), the applicable instrument, and a named reviewer. No map, no launch claim.
2. **AC-062 — Record the pinned WCAG version per instrument.** Each map row names the WCAG version and level the instrument pins, not just the instrument's name. Current pins from the research: EAA via EN 301 549 V3.2.1 → WCAG 2.1 AA; Section 508 → WCAG 2.0 AA; ADA Title II rule → WCAG 2.1 AA. A row that says only "EU — EAA" is incomplete.
3. **AC-063 — Applicability follows the user and the customer, never the developer.** The governing law is determined by where the users are, what sector the product is in, and who the customer is. The team's own location confers no obligations and no exemptions.
4. **AC-064 — Build to the newest; document against the pinned.** The build target stays WCAG 2.2 AA. Where an instrument pins an older version, conformance is additionally documented against that pinned version (2.2 removes only 4.1.1 Parsing, which a 2.0-pinned engagement still lists — record how it was treated, never silently skip it).
5. **AC-065 — State the technical result; never a legal verdict.** Deliverables state standard, version, level, scope, and date ("Evaluated against WCAG 2.1 Level AA, EN 301 549 scope, 2026-11-21"). They never state "ADA compliant", "EAA compliant", or "legally accessible". This skill gives engineering conformance guidance; it is not legal advice and guarantees no legal outcome.
6. **AC-066 — Escalate interpretation questions to D14/counsel.** Whether an instrument applies, what an exemption requires, and what exposure a gap creates are legal questions. Record each question in the map with the answer's source and date when D14/counsel provides it; engineering does not fill the gap with an assumption.
7. **AC-067 — Name the required conformance artifact per jurisdiction, with an owner.** Before launch, the map lists the artifact each jurisdiction or customer requires — an accessibility statement (WAD/EAA model), an ACR/VPAT for US procurement, or none — and names who produces and maintains it.
8. **AC-068 — The accessibility statement must match the audit.** A published statement contains: the conformance status from the latest accessibility-audit report, the known exceptions and non-accessible content, a working feedback/contact mechanism, and the preparation and review dates. Any claim beyond the audited scope, or any audited exception omitted, makes the statement false.
9. **AC-069 — The feedback mechanism is real, routed, and tested.** The statement's contact route reaches a named owner (monitored inbox or ticket queue), and a test barrier report is submitted and confirmed received before publication. A route nobody reads is recorded as a defect, not published as a mechanism.
10. **AC-070 — Exemptions are documented legal determinations, never engineering assumptions.** Disproportionate burden, fundamental alteration, and microenterprise carve-outs exist only as determinations recorded in the map with the determiner (D14/counsel), the evidence relied on, and the date. An engineer closing a finding "exempt" without that record has made a legal decision they cannot make.
11. **AC-071 — Re-map on scope change and on the review date.** A new market, a new sector, a government customer, or a change to an instrument (a revised EN 301 549 cited in the Official Journal, an ADA Title II date extension) triggers re-verification of the affected rows. Every map carries a review date; an expired review date means the map is stale, not still valid.
12. **AC-072 — Read procurement documents per engagement.** A contract can pin a WCAG version older than both the law's floor and the department target (a Section 508 contract pins 2.0) or require a specific artifact format. Record the contract's exact accessibility requirement in the map before any conformance promise is made in a bid or statement of work.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-031 — Bare compliance verdict.** Banned: writing "ADA compliant", "EAA compliant", "100% accessible", or "legally accessible" in any deliverable, page, badge, or bid. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: "Evaluated against WCAG 2.2 Level AA on 2026-11-21; per-criterion results in the audit report; legal applicability confirmed by D14." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-032 — Dead feedback route in the statement.** Banned: an accessibility statement whose feedback/contact link is a placeholder (`#`, an unbuilt page) or an address nobody monitors. Defeats: DET-UX-002. Instead: link a live contact route owned under AC-069, verified by the G-AC-034 test submission before publication. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-033 — Barrier-report form that submits nowhere.** Banned: a feedback form that shows a success message but stores and routes nothing, so reported barriers vanish. Defeats: DET-UX-003. Instead: persist the report to the support queue, return a reference the user can cite, and confirm receipt in the G-AC-034 live test. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-034 — Engineering-assumed exemption.** Banned: closing a barrier or skipping a required flow as "disproportionate burden", "out of scope", or "the vendor's widget" on an engineer's say-so. Defeats: DET-UX-013. Instead: keep the finding open and escalate under AC-066/AC-070; only a recorded D14/counsel determination with evidence can close it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-035 — Orphaned accessibility statement.** Banned: publishing the statement at a URL linked from nowhere — absent from the footer, help section, and sitemap — so users who need it cannot find it. Defeats: DET-UX-014. Instead: link the statement from the footer and help navigation on every page, and verify the link in the G-AC-033 check. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AC-031 — Jurisdiction map completeness (automated).** Verifies: AC-061, AC-062, AC-067. Check: run the project's map check over the legal file — `python3 scripts/check-jurisdiction-map.py docs/legal/jurisdiction-map.md` — which parses the map table and fails on any row with an empty jurisdiction, instrument, pinned WCAG version, level, required artifact, reviewer, or review-date field, and on any launch market with no row. Pass: zero missing fields and one complete row per launch market. Fail: block launch sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-032 — Pinned-version conformance documented.** Verifies: AC-064, AC-072. Check: for every map row whose pinned version is older than 2.2, confirm a conformance statement against that pinned version exists from the latest accessibility-audit (per-criterion results naming the pinned version), and that any contract-pinned requirement is quoted in the map. Pass: every pinned version has a matching dated conformance statement. Fail: block any external conformance claim for that jurisdiction. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-033 — Statement-vs-audit diff (automated).** Verifies: AC-068, BAN-AC-035. Check: extract the published statement's claimed conformance status, scope, and exception list; diff against the latest audit report's scope and findings register; also crawl the footer/help navigation for a working statement link. Pass: the statement claims nothing beyond the audited scope, every audited exception appears in the statement, and the statement link resolves. Fail: block publication (or unpublish) until the statement matches the audit. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-034 — Feedback route live test.** Verifies: AC-069. Check: submit a test barrier report through the exact route published in the statement; confirm it arrives with the named owner (ticket ID or inbox receipt) and note the elapsed time. Pass: receipt confirmed by the owner. Fail: block statement publication. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-035 — No-verdict language scan (automated).** Verifies: AC-065. Check: `grep -rniE "ADA compliant|EAA compliant|100% accessible|legally accessible|fully compliant" --include='*.md' --include='*.html' .` over deliverables and site copy, excluding quoted legal text and this skill's own BAN list. Pass: zero unaddressed hits — each hit is removed or rewritten as a technical result under AC-065. Fail: block release of the containing deliverable. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Map first: jurisdiction, instrument, pinned version, artifact, reviewer, review date.
- The law follows the user and the customer — never the developer.
- Build to 2.2 AA; document against the version the law or contract pins.
- Technical result only — "compliant" is a verdict engineering never issues.
- A statement that overclaims the audit is a false statement, not marketing.

## Checklist

- [ ] Jurisdiction map exists in the legal file set with one complete row per launch market (AC-061, G-AC-031).
- [ ] Every row pins a WCAG version and level and names its required conformance artifact and owner (AC-062, AC-067).
- [ ] Conformance is documented against each pinned older version, not only against 2.2 (AC-064, G-AC-032).
- [ ] No deliverable, page, or bid contains a legal verdict or blanket compliance claim (AC-065, G-AC-035).
- [ ] Accessibility statement matches the latest audit: status, scope, and every known exception (AC-068, G-AC-033).
- [ ] Feedback route is live, owned, and test-submitted before publication (AC-069, G-AC-034).
- [ ] Every exemption in force is a recorded D14/counsel determination with evidence and date (AC-070).
- [ ] Map carries a current review date and is re-verified on scope change (AC-071).

# inclusive-copy

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** WCAG 2.2 (criteria 2.4.4, 2.5.3, 3.3.1–3.3.3), W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ ; W3C WAI, "Writing for Web Accessibility" — https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/
- **Depends on:** internationalization (copy lives in its message catalogs), wcag (the criteria this copy standard serves)
- **Feeds into:** localization-workflow (translates this source copy), screen-readers (accessible names and announcements are this copy read aloud)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Writing or reviewing any words a user reads or hears — UI labels, buttons, links, instructions, error and empty-state copy, alt text, email and notification text — so the widest range of users can understand it and act on it, in the source language and in translation.
- **Do NOT use when:** Externalizing strings or wiring locale formatting (internationalization), running the translation pipeline (localization-workflow), or judging structural accessibility such as semantics, focus, and contrast (wcag, screen-readers, keyboard-accessibility).

## Rules

1. **AC-181 — Task copy is plain language.** Instructions, errors, and primary-flow text use common words and short sentences at a lower-secondary reading level. A term of art appears only when the task requires it, and is explained in the user's words at first use.
2. **AC-182 — One name per object, everywhere.** Every concept, object, and action carries the single term recorded in the project glossary — in navigation, buttons, errors, emails, help, and every translation. The same thing never appears under two names in one product (DET-CON-017).
3. **AC-183 — Link and button text stands alone.** Link text names its destination and button text names its action, so both make sense read out of context in a screen reader's link list (WCAG 2.4.4). The accessible name matches or contains the visible label (WCAG 2.5.3), so voice-control users can speak what they see.
4. **AC-184 — Error copy names the field, the problem, and the fix.** Each error is written in the user's terms, attached to the field it concerns, and says what to change (WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3). It never blames the user, never shows a bare code, and is never carried by color alone.
5. **AC-185 — Instructions and format hints come before the control.** Required formats, password rules, and constraints are stated before entry, not revealed by a failed submit (WCAG 3.3.2 practice; DET-UX-027). The user learns the rule before they can break it.
6. **AC-186 — Every state has words that say what happened and what is next.** Empty, loading, success, and failure states state the situation and the available action: an empty list explains why it is empty and how to fill it; a confirmation names what was actually done.
7. **AC-187 — No idiom, slang, or culture-specific metaphor carries meaning.** Copy is written literally, so it survives translation and reads plainly to users outside the source culture. A figure of speech is decoration only when the literal instruction stands complete without it.
8. **AC-188 — No ability-assuming or gendered-by-default language.** Copy does not assume how the user perceives or operates the product ("simply click", "see the report", "blind to errors"), and does not assign gender by default. Where a language requires gendered forms, they are chosen deliberately with MessageFormat `select`, never by accident.
9. **AC-189 — Alt text and captions are copy.** Alt text describes the image's content or purpose in the page; decorative images get empty `alt=""`. Alt text is never a file name, never "image of", and never a caption repeated word for word (DET-CON-027).
10. **AC-190 — The action comes first.** Instructions, headings, and errors front-load what the user must do or know; background and reasons follow. A user who reads only the first clause of each message can still complete the task.
11. **AC-191 — Formality is a per-locale decision.** Each locale's style guide records its politeness and formality level (e.g., German Sie/du, Spanish tú/usted), and translations are reviewed against it. The source language's level of familiarity is never imposed on a locale by default.
12. **AC-192 — Destructive-action copy names the object and the consequence.** The explanation states what will be deleted or changed and whether it can be undone; the confirm button repeats the action ("Delete project"), never a bare "Yes" or "OK" whose meaning depends on reading the dialog.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-091 — "Click here" and other context-free link text.** Banned: link or button text that names the gesture instead of the destination or action — "click here", "tap here", "learn more", "this page". Defeats: DET-UX-002. Instead: "Download the March invoice (PDF)" — text that names the destination and stands alone. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-092 — Generic, coded, or blaming error messages.** Banned: errors that state no field, no problem, and no fix — "Invalid input", "Error 422", "You failed to enter a valid date", "Something went wrong" as the whole message. Defeats: DET-UX-006. Instead: "Card expiry — this date is in the past. Enter a future date in MM/YY format." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-093 — Placeholder text as the only label.** Banned: a form field whose placeholder is its sole label or instruction, so the label vanishes on entry and is never announced as a name. Defeats: DET-UX-022. Instead: a persistent visible label "Start date" plus the hint "Format: DD/MM/YYYY" beside the field, before entry. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-094 — Directions that point at color alone.** Banned: copy that locates information by color — "fix the fields marked in red", "press the green button", "items in orange are overdue". Defeats: DET-UX-021. Instead: name the field and the state in words — "Email address — this address is already registered" — with color as a redundant cue only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-095 — Generic filler in place of an instruction.** Banned: marketing filler and AI-vocabulary padding where the user needs a fact or an action — "supercharge your workflow with our cutting-edge, seamless solution". Defeats: DET-CON-006. Instead: "Import a CSV file up to 10 MB. Columns: name, email, signup date." Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AC-091 — Banned-pattern lint over the catalogs.** Verifies: AC-183, AC-184, AC-189. Check: grep the message catalogs for the banned patterns — `grep -rniE "click here|tap here|learn more|read more"` over link/button keys; error-message keys matching bare codes (`error [0-9]{3}` with no other text) or color-only references (`marked in red|shown in red|green button`); alt-text values matching file-name patterns (`\.(png|jpe?g|svg)$`). Pass: zero findings. Fail: block shipment; rewrite each hit to the rule it violates and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-092 — Reading-level scan of primary flows.** Verifies: AC-181, AC-190. Check: extract the source-locale strings of the primary flows (onboarding, checkout, the top task per product area) plus all error strings into a plain-text file and run a readability scorer (e.g., `textstat` Flesch-Kincaid grade). Pass: task copy scores at or below the project's agreed grade ceiling (default: grade 9); every string above it is rewritten or listed in progress.md with a written justification (e.g., a legally fixed term). Fail: block shipment for unrewritten, unjustified strings. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-093 — Glossary conformance check.** Verifies: AC-182. Check: run the TMS/catalog glossary check (or a scripted term scan) comparing catalog strings against the project glossary's approved terms and its recorded do-not-use synonyms. Pass: zero do-not-use synonyms and zero concepts appearing under two names. Fail: block shipment; unify on the glossary term in every surface, including emails and help. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-094 — Human plain-language review of flows and errors.** Verifies: AC-184, AC-185, AC-186, AC-190. Check: a reviewer who did not write the copy reads (a) every primary-flow string in order, (b) every error string triggered by deliberately failing each form, and (c) the link/button text as an out-of-context list. Pass: the reviewer can state, for each error, the field, problem, and fix without seeing the screen, and can predict each link's destination from its text alone; sign-off recorded. Fail: return failing strings to the author; the release does not proceed on the reviewer's "probably fine". Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-095 — Per-locale idiom and formality review.** Verifies: AC-187, AC-188, AC-191. Check: for each shipping locale, the locale reviewer checks the translated primary-flow and error strings against the locale style guide — formality level consistent throughout, no source idiom carried over literally, gendered forms deliberate. Pass: reviewer sign-off per locale with zero unresolved idiom or formality findings. Fail: block shipment for that locale only; other locales are unaffected. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- If a link list can't explain it, the link text failed.
- Every error: field, problem, fix — in the user's words, before blame, without a code.
- One thing, one name — the glossary term, on every surface, in every language.
- Say it literally: if an idiom carries the meaning, translation will drop it.
- Instructions before the control; the action before the explanation.

## Checklist

- [ ] Link and button text names its destination or action and stands alone out of context — G-AC-091 lint is clean.
- [ ] Every error message names the field, states the problem, and gives the fix; no bare codes, no blame, no color-only references.
- [ ] Required formats and constraints are stated before the control, not revealed by failure.
- [ ] Empty, loading, success, and failure states each say what happened and what to do next.
- [ ] Every concept uses its single glossary term on all surfaces — G-AC-093 check is clean.
- [ ] No idiom, slang, or ability-assuming phrase carries meaning in shipped copy.
- [ ] Alt text describes content or purpose; decorative images use empty `alt=""`; no file names.
- [ ] Primary-flow copy passed the reading-level scan (G-AC-092) and the human plain-language review (G-AC-094).
- [ ] Each shipping locale has a recorded formality level and a signed idiom/formality review — G-AC-095.

# internationalization

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** ICU, Unicode — https://icu.unicode.org/home ; Unicode CLDR plural rules — https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules ; WCAG 2.2 (criteria 3.1.1, 3.1.2), W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- **Depends on:** wcag (the `lang` requirements this skill implements are WCAG 3.1.1/3.1.2)
- **Feeds into:** localization-workflow (consumes the catalogs and context notes), rtl-layouts (consumes correct `lang`/`dir` metadata), inclusive-copy

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Engineering the source product so a new locale is data, not a code change — extracting strings into catalogs, wiring ICU MessageFormat and `Intl` formatting, setting `lang`/`dir`, and designing layout that survives translation. This skill owns engineering readiness: strings, formats, layout flexibility.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running the translation process itself — string freezes, translator handoff, review, fallback policy per string class (that is localization-workflow), doing direction-specific layout and mirroring work (rtl-layouts), or writing the source copy's wording (inclusive-copy).

## Rules

1. **AC-121 — Every user-facing string lives in a message catalog.** UI copy, emails, notifications, error messages, alt text, and PDF templates are externalized into catalogs keyed by meaning (e.g. `checkout.payButton`), never by English text or screen position. A user-facing literal in component code is a defect, not a shortcut.
2. **AC-122 — Whole messages are the unit of translation.** Any string with plurals, gender, lists, or embedded values is one ICU MessageFormat message. Word order is a property of the locale, so a sentence is never assembled from translated fragments.
3. **AC-123 — Plurals come from CLDR categories, never from code branches.** Plural and ordinal selection uses MessageFormat plural/selectordinal or `Intl.PluralRules`, driven by Unicode CLDR rules (Japanese uses one category, English two, Polish four, Arabic six). Code passes the raw count; it never tests `count == 1`.
4. **AC-124 — All formatting goes through locale APIs.** Dates, times, numbers, currencies, units, lists, and relative time ("in 3 days") are formatted with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.NumberFormat`, `Intl.ListFormat`, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` (or ICU4J/ICU4C equivalents) for the active locale, with the time zone stated explicitly where it matters. No value is formatted by string concatenation.
5. **AC-125 — Formatting is not conversion.** An amount is displayed in its own currency via `Intl.NumberFormat` with that currency code. The display layer never converts currency, units, or time zones silently; conversion happens only where the product explicitly defines it, and the result is labeled as converted.
6. **AC-126 — Every document and language change carries correct `lang` and `dir`.** Each page sets a valid BCP 47 `lang` on the root element and `dir` matching the locale's direction; inline passages in another language carry their own `lang` (WCAG 3.1.1, 3.1.2 — this is also how screen readers choose pronunciation). Direction is declared, never guessed from the text content.
7. **AC-127 — Language switching changes the whole experience.** Selecting a locale changes all UI strings, formats, sort order, and direction together — never body copy alone with English buttons, dates, and errors left behind.
8. **AC-128 — Locale behavior is data, not constants.** Sort order (via `Intl.Collator`), calendars, first day of week, numbering system, and name/address field order come from CLDR-backed locale data or explicit per-locale configuration — never from hard-coded arrays in code.
9. **AC-129 — Layout is designed for expansion and contraction.** Containers flex with text length: no fixed-width text buttons, no fixed-height single-line labels without an overflow behavior, and no text baked into images or canvas. Translated strings may run substantially longer or shorter than the source; the layout must absorb both.
10. **AC-130 — Fallback chains are explicit and visible in staging.** Each locale declares its fallback chain (e.g. `ar-EG` → `ar` → source locale). In staging builds, an untranslated string renders visibly marked as fallback so gaps are found before release; production fallback follows the policy localization-workflow sets per string class.
11. **AC-131 — Every string ships with a translator context note.** At authoring time, each catalog entry records where it appears, what its placeholders mean, and any character limit. A string a translator cannot interpret from the catalog alone is unfinished.
12. **AC-132 — Pseudo-localization runs before real translation.** A pseudo-locale build (expanded, accented, bracketed strings) is rendered and checked for hard-coded text (which stays in the source language), truncation, overflow, and mojibake before any translator is engaged.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-061 — Hard-coded user-facing string in a component.** Banned: a literal such as `<button>Save changes</button>` or an English error string embedded in code instead of a catalog key. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: every string is a catalog key (`settings.deleteDialog.title`) resolved through the message system, so all screens localize together. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-062 — Sentence built by string concatenation.** Banned: assembling a message from fragments, e.g. `t('youHave') + ' ' + n + ' ' + t('newMessages')`. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: one MessageFormat message — `You have {count, plural, one {# new message} other {# new messages}}` — translated as a unit per locale. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-063 — Plural chosen by a `count == 1` branch in code.** Banned: `count === 1 ? t('item') : t('items')` or any code-side plural branching. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: pass the raw count to a MessageFormat plural (or `Intl.PluralRules`) and let CLDR categories select the form. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-064 — Hand-rolled date, number, or currency formatting.** Banned: formatting by concatenation or fixed pattern (`month + '/' + day + '/' + year`, `'$' + amount.toFixed(2)`), parsing user input against one hard-coded format, or converting a price to another currency in the display layer. Defeats: DET-UX-027. Instead: format and parse through `Intl`/ICU for the active locale, state the expected format beside the field, and display amounts in their own currency. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-065 — Text baked into an image or locked in a fixed-width box.** Banned: headlines, labels, or button text rendered into image/canvas assets, or text containers with fixed pixel widths/heights and no overflow behavior. Defeats: DET-UX-023. Instead: real text in flexible containers, checked in the pseudo-localization render (G-AC-062); images carry no words the user must read. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-061 — Hard-coded string scan.** Verifies: AC-121, AC-124. Check: run the project lint/grep over UI source for user-facing literals outside catalog imports (JSX text nodes, string literals passed to rendering, template text), e.g. the i18n lint rule set plus `grep -rn` spot patterns agreed for the stack; also grep for hand-rolled formatters (`toFixed(` in view code, manual month/day concatenation, custom date-format functions). Pass: zero findings in both scans. Fail: block shipment; each finding is externalized or routed through `Intl` before re-check. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-062 — Pseudo-localization render.** Verifies: AC-129, AC-132, AC-121. Check: build with the pseudo-locale (expanded, accented, bracketed) and screenshot every primary screen and primary flow; inspect each shot for text still in the source language (hard-coded), clipped or overflowing strings, and mojibake. Pass: no source-language leftovers, no truncation or overflow on any primary screen. Fail: block shipment; fix the string or the container and re-render. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-063 — Locale metadata and switch test.** Verifies: AC-126, AC-127, AC-130. Check: for each supported locale, load the primary pages and assert the root `lang` is the correct BCP 47 tag, `dir` matches the locale, a language switch re-renders strings, formats, and direction together, and one deliberately untranslated key in staging renders with the visible fallback marking. Pass: all assertions hold for every supported locale. Fail: block shipment for the failing locale. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-064 — Message and context-note review.** Verifies: AC-122, AC-123, AC-131. Check: manual review of the catalog diff for the release — every new or changed entry is a whole MessageFormat message (no fragments), plurals use CLDR categories, and each entry carries a context note with placeholder meanings and limits. Pass: reviewer signs off with zero fragment messages and zero missing context notes. Fail: return entries to the author; the catalog does not go to localization-workflow. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Localization is data, not code changes: if a new locale needs a developer, the engineering failed.
- Whole messages are translated; fragments and concatenation break word order.
- Code never branches on count — CLDR owns plurals.
- Format with `Intl`, in the amount's own currency: formatting is not conversion.
- `lang` and `dir` on every page — declared, never guessed.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every user-facing string (UI, email, errors, alt text, PDFs) resolves from a catalog key — G-AC-061 scan is clean.
- [ ] No sentence is built by concatenation; strings with values are whole ICU MessageFormat messages.
- [ ] Plurals and ordinals use CLDR categories via MessageFormat/`Intl.PluralRules`; no `count == 1` branch exists.
- [ ] Dates, numbers, currencies, units, and relative time all format through `Intl`/ICU for the active locale.
- [ ] No display-layer currency conversion; amounts show in their own currency.
- [ ] Root `lang` (BCP 47) and `dir` are correct per locale, and inline language changes carry their own `lang`.
- [ ] Pseudo-localization render passed with no source-language leftovers, truncation, or overflow — G-AC-062.
- [ ] Every catalog entry carries a translator context note with placeholder meanings and limits.

<!-- generated from skills/accessibility-i18n/keyboard-accessibility/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# keyboard-accessibility

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG), W3C — https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/ ; WCAG 2.2, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- **Depends on:** wcag (fixes the WCAG 2.2 AA target this skill builds to)
- **Feeds into:** accessibility-audit, accessibility-testing, screen-readers

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Building or fixing any interactive UI — navigation, forms, dialogs, menus, custom widgets, drag interactions — so every function is reachable and operable with keyboard alone, in a visible, logical order.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running a scoped conformance evaluation (accessibility-audit finds and records; this skill fixes), testing with a screen reader (screen-readers), or deciding pointer target sizes (wcag / the design system — this skill covers keyboard operation only).

## Rules

1. **AC-081 — Native interactive elements first.** Use `<button>`, `<a href>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, and `<textarea>` for anything interactive; they bring focusability, key handling, and roles for free. A custom widget is built only when no native element fits, and then it implements the APG keyboard model for its pattern in full (AC-089).
2. **AC-082 — Everything operable by pointer is operable by keyboard alone (WCAG 2.1.1).** Every action a mouse or touch user can perform — open, close, submit, sort, filter, delete, drag — is reachable by Tab/Shift+Tab and activatable with Enter and/or Space as the element's pattern requires. If a function has no keyboard path, it does not ship.
3. **AC-083 — No keyboard trap anywhere (WCAG 2.1.2).** Focus can always move away from every component using only the keyboard, including embedded third-party widgets (chat, payment, video iframes). The one exception is a modal dialog, which holds focus only while open and releases it on close (AC-088).
4. **AC-084 — Focus order follows the visual and logical reading order (WCAG 2.4.3).** Tab order comes from DOM order, which is arranged to match the reading order. Positive `tabindex` values (any value above 0) are forbidden — `tabindex="0"` and `tabindex="-1"` are the only permitted values.
5. **AC-085 — The focus indicator is always visible (WCAG 2.4.7).** Every interactive element shows a clear focus indicator in every state (hover, active, disabled-adjacent). The browser outline is never removed unless replaced in the same change by an indicator of equal or better visibility (contrast and thickness) applied via `:focus-visible` or an equivalent.
6. **AC-086 — Focus is never fully obscured by sticky chrome (WCAG 2.4.11).** A focused element must not be entirely hidden by sticky headers, cookie banners, or chat widgets. Sticky elements are paired with `scroll-margin-top` (or the inline equivalent) on focusable content so a scrolled-to focused element clears the chrome.
7. **AC-087 — A bypass block precedes repeated navigation (WCAG 2.4.1).** Every page with repeated navigation opens with a skip link ("Skip to main content") as the first focusable element; it is visible on focus and activating it moves focus to the main content region, not merely scrolls to it.
8. **AC-088 — Dialogs manage focus deliberately.** On open, focus moves into the dialog (first focusable element or the dialog itself); while open, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle inside it; Esc closes it; on close, focus returns to the element that invoked it. A dialog that drops focus to the document body on close fails this rule.
9. **AC-089 — Composite widgets follow the APG keyboard model exactly.** Inside tabs, menus, listboxes, grids, and toolbars, arrow keys move between items, Tab moves into and out of the component as one stop, Home/End jump to the ends, and Esc closes and returns focus to the trigger. Do not invent a per-project key model.
10. **AC-090 — Focus moves on route change or content replacement only by decision.** After a route change, focus lands on a deliberate target (the page heading or main region with `tabindex="-1"`). After dynamic insertion or removal, focus stays on the invoking control or moves to the inserted content's logical start — never silently resets to the top of the document while the user is mid-task.
11. **AC-091 — Every drag or pointer gesture has a keyboard equivalent.** Sliders respond to arrow keys, sortable lists offer keyboard move commands (e.g. select with Space, move with arrows, drop with Space), and drag-to-reorder, drag-to-resize, and drawing surfaces each ship a non-drag path to the same result.
12. **AC-092 — Character-key shortcuts are off by default or remappable (WCAG 2.1.4).** Single printable-character shortcuts are active only when the relevant component has focus, or can be turned off or remapped by the user. Shortcuts never override browser or assistive-technology keys.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-041 — Keyboard trap.** Banned: any component — including a third-party embed — that focus can enter but cannot leave with the keyboard alone. Defeats: DET-UX-016. Instead: fix or configure the embed so focus exits with Tab/Shift+Tab (or Esc), and verify it in the keyboard walk before launch. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-042 — Removed or invisible focus indicator.** Banned: `outline: none` (or `outline: 0`) on interactive elements, or a custom focus style too faint to see, shipped for looks. Defeats: DET-UX-018. Instead: keep the native outline or supply a visible `:focus-visible` indicator of equal or better contrast and thickness (AC-085). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-043 — Pointer-only control.** Banned: an interactive element that responds only to mouse/touch — a clickable `<div>` with a click handler, or a menu that opens only on hover — with no focus stop and no key operation. Defeats: DET-UX-001. Instead: use a native `<button>` or link, or implement the full APG pattern with focusability, key handling, role, and name. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-044 — Dialog that strands focus.** Banned: a modal that, on close, leaves focus on the removed element or resets it to the document body, so the keyboard user restarts from the page top. Defeats: DET-UX-017. Instead: store the invoking element on open and restore focus to it on close (AC-088). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-045 — Undismissable modal.** Banned: a modal, lightbox, or interstitial that cannot be closed with the keyboard (no Esc handling and no focusable close control). Defeats: DET-UX-028. Instead: support Esc and provide a labeled, focusable close button reachable in the dialog's tab cycle. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-041 — Positive-tabindex and outline lint (automated).** Verifies: AC-084, AC-085. Check: run `grep -rnE 'tabindex="[1-9][0-9]*"|tabIndex=\{[1-9]' src/` (must return zero matches) and the project's CSS lint rule flagging `outline: none|0` on `:focus` selectors with no replacement indicator in the same rule block. Pass: zero positive tabindex values and zero unreplaced outline removals in the codebase. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-042 — Scripted Tab-order walk (automated).** Verifies: AC-082, AC-084, AC-085, AC-086. Check: a Playwright script loads each primary page, presses Tab repeatedly, and records `document.activeElement` at each stop; assert (a) every interactive element in the page is reached, (b) the stop sequence matches the DOM/reading order, and (c) each focused element's computed style shows a visible indicator (non-`none` outline, box-shadow, or border change) and its bounding box is not fully covered by sticky chrome. Pass: all assertions green on all primary pages. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-043 — No-mouse journey completion (manual).** Verifies: AC-082, AC-091. Check: with the mouse disconnected or pointer input disabled, complete each primary journey (register, search → detail, add to cart → checkout, submit a form with an error and correct it) using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys, and Esc. Pass: every journey completes with no step requiring a pointer and no drag action lacking a keyboard equivalent. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-044 — Dialog focus test.** Verifies: AC-083, AC-088. Check: for every dialog, menu, and lightbox: open it from the keyboard; confirm focus lands inside it; Tab through a full cycle and confirm focus stays inside; close with Esc and confirm focus is back on the invoking element; repeat for any third-party embed, confirming focus can also leave it. Pass: all dialogs pass all four steps. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-045 — Skip-link check.** Verifies: AC-087. Check: on every page template, press Tab once from the top of the page: the skip link must be the first stop and visible; activate it and confirm focus (not just scroll position) moves into the main content, so the next Tab lands on the first main-content control. Pass: every template passes. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- If a mouse can do it, the keyboard can do it — or it does not ship.
- Tab order is DOM order; positive tabindex is banned.
- Never remove the outline without a better one in the same change.
- Dialogs: focus in on open, trapped while open, returned on close.
- First Tab stop on every page: the skip link.

## Checklist

- [ ] All interactive elements are native elements or full APG-pattern widgets (AC-081, AC-089).
- [ ] Every pointer operation, including drag, has a working keyboard path (AC-082, AC-091).
- [ ] No keyboard trap exists anywhere, including third-party embeds (AC-083).
- [ ] Lint is clean: zero positive tabindex values, zero unreplaced outline removals (AC-084, AC-085, G-AC-041).
- [ ] Scripted Tab-order walk passes on all primary pages, focus visible and unobscured at every stop (G-AC-042, AC-086).
- [ ] Primary journeys completed with no mouse (G-AC-043).
- [ ] Every dialog traps focus while open, closes with Esc, and returns focus to its invoker (AC-088, G-AC-044).
- [ ] Skip link is the first Tab stop on every template and moves focus to main content (AC-087, G-AC-045).

<!-- generated from skills/accessibility-i18n/localization-workflow/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# localization-workflow

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** ICU MessageFormat documentation, Unicode — https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/ ; Unicode CLDR — https://cldr.unicode.org/
- **Depends on:** internationalization (produces the catalogs, ICU messages, and translator context notes this workflow moves through the pipeline)
- **Feeds into:** rtl-layouts (translated RTL locales enter direction and per-script layout verification), accessibility-audit (localized builds and flows are audit scope)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Running the translation process for a release — string freeze, translator handoff with context, automated import checks, in-context and native-speaker review, fallback policy, and the per-locale release decision. This skill owns the process: extraction, translation, review, QA, release.
- **Do NOT use when:** Engineering the source product for localization — catalog structure, ICU MessageFormat authoring, `Intl` formatting, layout flexibility (that is internationalization), doing RTL mirroring and per-script layout QA (rtl-layouts), or deciding the source copy's wording and reading level (inclusive-copy).

## Rules

1. **AC-141 — Localization runs as a pipeline with tracked states, not correspondence.** Each string moves through extraction → freeze → handoff → translation → automated checks → in-context review → release, and its state per locale is visible in the translation management system (TMS) or catalog tooling. A string whose state nobody can state is not in the pipeline, whatever an email thread says.
2. **AC-142 — Source strings freeze per release.** At the freeze point the release's key set and source text are fixed; translators work against the frozen set. Strings authored after the freeze belong to the next release unless they pass AC-150 change control.
3. **AC-143 — Every handoff ships translator context.** Each string goes out with its context note from the catalog (where it appears, what each placeholder means), a screenshot or screen reference, any character or byte limit, the project glossary, and the do-not-translate list (product names, legal names, code-like tokens). A string sent without context is sent back, not guessed at.
4. **AC-144 — Placeholder and ICU integrity is machine-checked on every import.** Every imported message is parsed as ICU MessageFormat and its placeholder set (names, types, plural/select structure) is compared against the source message. A mismatch or an unparsable message fails the build — it is never a typo to fix later.
5. **AC-145 — Key parity is enforced per locale.** Every locale catalog carries every source key. A missing key in a primary locale is a release blocker for primary flows; elsewhere it follows the fallback policy in AC-151 and is counted in the release report, never silently absent.
6. **AC-146 — Translation memory and the glossary are maintained as project assets.** Approved translations are reused through translation memory, product terms follow the glossary in every locale, and the do-not-translate list is honored exactly. The same concept never appears under two translated names in one locale.
7. **AC-147 — Machine translation is labeled and never ships unreviewed.** MT output is marked as MT in the pipeline wherever it is used as a draft. Native-speaker human review is mandatory before release for legal, payment, health, and safety strings, and for all primary-flow strings; MT alone never satisfies review for those classes.
8. **AC-148 — Every locale has a named human reviewer, and review happens in context.** "The vendor delivered it" is not review. The named reviewer walks the primary flows on a staging build in the real UI — real layout, real data lengths, real error paths — and signs off per locale; string-list proofreading alone does not sign off a locale.
9. **AC-149 — Length and expansion risk are flagged at translation time.** Translations are checked against the character/byte limits recorded in the context notes as they are delivered, and over-limit strings are resolved with the translator (shorter wording, approved abbreviation) before layout QA — overflow is not discovered by a screenshot at the end.
10. **AC-150 — A post-freeze source change invalidates that key's translations.** Any change to a frozen source string marks its translations in every locale as stale until re-translated or re-checked against the new source. The changed key ships in a locale only after that re-check; the old translation never rides along by default.
11. **AC-151 — Fallback is explicit, visible, and honestly claimed.** Each locale declares its fallback chain. In staging, untranslated strings render visibly marked as fallback. In production, fallback follows the recorded per-string-class policy, and any source-language content shown to users is marked as such — never silently presented as translated. A locale is claimed "supported" only when its UI, taxonomy, search, formatting, RTL, and descriptions have each passed their gates.
12. **AC-152 — Each locale's support tier is recorded and matches every public claim.** The project files record a tier per locale (full / UI-only / best-effort) with the release validation report: keys translated, checks passed, reviewer sign-offs. Help pages, marketing copy, and sales answers cite the tier; a best-effort locale is never described as fully supported.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-071 — Machine translation shipped without human review.** Banned: MT output released as final copy, above all on legal, payment, health, safety, or primary-flow strings. Defeats: DET-UX-006. Instead: MT is labeled as a draft in the pipeline and passes native-speaker review (AC-147) before release; unreviewed MT stays out of the build. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-072 — Translations imported without placeholder/ICU validation.** Banned: accepting a locale file whose messages were never parsed or compared against the source placeholders. Defeats: DET-UX-010. Instead: every import runs the G-AC-071 parse-and-compare check; a broken message fails the build and returns to the translator. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-073 — Silent fallback presented as a translated locale.** Banned: serving source-language strings in production with no marking while the locale is listed as supported. Defeats: DET-UX-015. Instead: fallback follows AC-151 — visibly marked in staging, policy-governed and source-marked in production, and the locale's claim matches its recorded tier (AC-152). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-074 — Translation accepted with no length check against its limits.** Banned: delivering strings whose recorded character/byte limits were never checked, leaving expansion to layout QA. Defeats: DET-UX-023. Instead: limits travel with the string (AC-143) and are enforced at delivery (AC-149, G-AC-072); over-limit strings are reworded before layout QA. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-075 — Post-freeze source change shipped over stale translations.** Banned: editing a frozen source string and releasing while locales still carry the translation of the old text. Defeats: DET-UX-013. Instead: the change invalidates the key in every locale (AC-150); it re-enters translation and ships only after re-check. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-071 — Key-parity and placeholder-integrity check (automated).** Verifies: AC-144, AC-145. Check: run the catalog validation script over every locale file for the release: diff each locale's key set against the frozen source key set, parse every message with the ICU MessageFormat parser, and compare each message's placeholder names/types and plural/select structure against the source message. Pass: zero missing keys in primary locales, zero unparsable messages, zero placeholder mismatches across all locales. Fail: block shipment; offending keys return to translation and are re-imported. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-072 — Length-limit check (automated).** Verifies: AC-143, AC-149. Check: for every catalog entry carrying a character or byte limit in its context note, compare each locale's delivered string length against the limit and produce an over-limit report per locale. Pass: zero over-limit strings in primary flows; any elsewhere are individually waived in writing by the locale reviewer. Fail: block shipment for the affected locale until strings are reworded and re-checked. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-073 — Visible-fallback check (automated + staging walk).** Verifies: AC-151, AC-152. Check: in the staging build, force one deliberately untranslated key per locale and confirm it renders with the visible fallback marking; then inspect the production configuration and confirm fallback follows the recorded per-string-class policy and the locale's public claim matches its recorded support tier. Pass: marking renders in staging for every locale, and no production locale claims a tier above its record. Fail: block shipment for the mis-claimed or unmarked locale. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-074 — In-context review sign-off (manual).** Verifies: AC-147, AC-148. Check: the named reviewer for each locale walks the primary flows on the staging build in that locale — including one error path and one empty state — and records sign-off; legal, payment, health, and safety strings additionally carry native-speaker review evidence, and any MT-drafted string in those classes shows its review record. Pass: sign-off recorded for every shipping locale, with review evidence for every critical string class. Fail: the locale does not ship; it waits for review or drops to a lower recorded tier. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- A pipeline with states, not an email with a spreadsheet.
- Broken placeholder, broken build — integrity is machine-checked, never eyeballed.
- Machine translation is a draft with a label, never a reviewer.
- Fallback is visible or it is a false claim: supported means every surface passed.
- Change the source, invalidate the translations — stale strings never ride along.

## Checklist

- [ ] Source strings are frozen for the release and the frozen key set is the one translators received — AC-142.
- [ ] Every handed-off string carried its context note, screenshot/screen reference, limits, glossary, and do-not-translate list — AC-143.
- [ ] G-AC-071 passed: zero missing keys in primary locales, zero unparsable messages, zero placeholder mismatches.
- [ ] G-AC-072 passed: no over-limit strings in primary flows; waivers elsewhere are written and signed.
- [ ] Every locale has a named reviewer; MT-drafted strings are labeled, and legal/payment/health/safety strings carry native-speaker review — AC-147, AC-148.
- [ ] G-AC-074 sign-off is recorded per locale from an in-context staging walk, error path included.
- [ ] Post-freeze source changes invalidated their keys in all locales and were re-checked before shipping — AC-150.
- [ ] Staging fallback renders visibly marked, production fallback matches the recorded policy, and each locale's public claim matches its recorded support tier — AC-151, AC-152, G-AC-073.

<!-- generated from skills/accessibility-i18n/reduced-motion/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# reduced-motion

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** WCAG 2.2 criteria 2.2.2, 2.3.1, 2.3.3, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ ; `prefers-reduced-motion`, MDN — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion
- **Depends on:** wcag (this skill operationalizes its motion criteria)
- **Feeds into:** accessibility-audit, accessibility-testing, motion, scroll-experiences

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** A product contains any motion — scroll animations, parallax, carousels, auto-playing media, page transitions, animated counters or charts — and needs a reduced-motion behavior for each, plus the normative motion floors (flash, pause/stop) verified before release.
- **Do NOT use when:** Designing the motion itself (motion and scroll-experiences own the design; this skill constrains it), running the full conformance evaluation (accessibility-audit), or judging non-motion visual criteria such as contrast (wcag).

## Rules

1. **AC-101 — The OS setting is an instruction, not a hint.** `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is a user instruction delivered through the operating system. When it is set, every non-essential animation in the product is removed or replaced; no component, page, or third-party embed may opt out individually.
2. **AC-102 — One global CSS block neutralizes decorative motion.** A single global `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block disables decorative `@keyframes` animation and transitions (or reduces them to instant state changes / short crossfades) and turns off smooth scrolling (`scroll-behavior: auto`). Per-component overrides of this block are defects.
3. **AC-103 — JavaScript motion checks the same signal.** JS-driven motion — scroll listeners, IntersectionObserver animations, canvas/WebGL loops, animation libraries, animated counters — reads `window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` before starting and subscribes to its change event, so a mid-session OS change takes effect without a reload. CSS coverage alone is not coverage.
4. **AC-104 — Inventory every motion, assign each a behavior.** Before release, the motion inventory lists every animated element (scroll reveals, parallax, carousels, auto-playing media, page transitions, counters, loading animations) with its reduced-motion behavior: remove, replace with an instant change, replace with a crossfade, or gate behind explicit user activation. An unlisted animation is an unreviewed animation.
5. **AC-105 — Auto-playing media is pausable in every mode.** Any video, carousel, or animated image that starts automatically and lasts more than five seconds ships with a visible pause/stop control, in reduced-motion mode and in full-motion mode alike (WCAG 2.2.2). Under reduced motion, auto-play does not start at all; the user starts it deliberately or not at all.
6. **AC-106 — Nothing flashes above the threshold.** No content flashes more than three times in any one-second period (WCAG 2.3.1). This applies to video, animated images, ad slots, and transition effects, and it applies in every motion mode — reduced-motion settings are not the control for seizure risk.
7. **AC-107 — Animation is never the only carrier of meaning.** Every state change an animation shows — step completed, item added, error arrived, progress advanced — also changes text, an icon, or an ARIA state, so the change is fully communicated when the animation is removed. If deleting the animation deletes information, the design fails this rule.
8. **AC-108 — Essential motion stays minimal and vestibular-safe.** Motion that is itself the information (a progress indicator, a map zoom the user drives) may remain under reduced motion, reduced to the minimum: no parallax, no zooming or panning of large screen areas, no spinning, no motion that simulates camera movement through space.
9. **AC-109 — Interaction-triggered animation can be disabled.** Non-essential animation triggered by interaction (hover effects, click ripples, animated route transitions) is disabled under reduced motion, per WCAG 2.3.3 — adopted as department practice even though the criterion is AAA and the baseline is AA.
10. **AC-110 — New motion is justified like new copy.** A design review that adds motion states, in the same ticket, what the motion communicates and its reduced-motion equivalent from AC-104's behavior list. Motion with no stated purpose is removed, not accommodated.
11. **AC-111 — Reduced motion never removes function.** The reduced-motion experience completes every task the full-motion experience completes, in the same number of steps: content revealed by scroll animation is present without the animation, carousel slides are reachable without auto-advance, and nothing waits on an animation finishing to become usable.
12. **AC-112 — Third-party embeds are in scope.** Embedded players, chat widgets, ad slots, and social feeds are checked under reduced-motion emulation like first-party code. An embed that cannot honor the setting is replaced, wrapped behind explicit user activation, or recorded as a finding with the vendor named — never silently shipped.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-051 — CSS-only reduced-motion coverage.** Banned: shipping a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block while JavaScript-driven parallax, scroll animations, or animated counters keep running untouched. Defeats: DET-VIS-041. Instead: gate every JS animation on `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` per AC-103 and verify under emulation per G-AC-051. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-052 — Auto-play with no pause control.** Banned: auto-playing video, carousels, or animated heroes that start on load and offer no visible pause/stop control, in any motion mode. Defeats: DET-VIS-041. Instead: ship a visible pause button per AC-105, and under reduced motion do not auto-start or auto-advance at all. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-053 — Flashing content above the WCAG threshold.** Banned: any content — video, animated image, ad creative, transition effect — that flashes more than three times in one second. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Instead: remove the strobe; draw attention with a static badge or a single slow crossfade, and run the flash check in G-AC-052 before publication. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-054 — Animation as the only signal of a state change.** Banned: communicating a completed action, error, or progress change solely by animation, with no text, icon, or ARIA change. Defeats: DET-UX-011. Instead: pair the animation with a persistent signal per AC-107 (cart count text updates, a polite live-region announcement, a visible confirmation). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-055 — One global scroll animation applied to everything.** Banned: a single library-default fade-up (or equivalent) applied uniformly to every section on scroll, with no per-element purpose and no reduced-motion removal. Defeats: DET-VIS-040. Instead: animate selectively where motion explains a change (AC-110), and remove scroll reveals entirely under reduced motion per AC-102/AC-104. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AC-051 — Reduced-motion emulation run (automated).** Verifies: AC-101, AC-102, AC-103, AC-104. Check: run the primary flows in Playwright with `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` emulation (or browser devtools emulation), with a script asserting no element on each primary page has a running CSS animation or auto-playing media, and grep the built CSS/JS for the media query and for animation entry points lacking a `matchMedia` gate. Pass: zero non-essential animations running and zero un-gated animation entry points. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-052 — Flash and pause-control check (automated + manual).** Verifies: AC-105, AC-106. Check: scripted DOM pass asserting every auto-playing `video`/`carousel` element has an associated visible pause/stop control; manual/tool-assisted flash review of every video and animated image before publication, counting flashes per second. Pass: every auto-playing element is pausable and no content exceeds three flashes per second. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-053 — Reduced-motion task walk (manual).** Verifies: AC-107, AC-111. Check: with reduced motion emulated, complete each primary process end to end and confirm every state change is communicated by text, icon, or ARIA state, and every task completes in the same number of steps as in full-motion mode. Pass: a dated walk record lists each primary process as pass/fail with no missing-signal findings. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-054 — Motion inventory complete.** Verifies: AC-104, AC-110, AC-112. Check: diff the motion inventory against the shipped build's animated components (from the G-AC-051 scan output); confirm every shipped animation, including third-party embeds, has an inventory row with an assigned reduced-motion behavior. Pass: zero shipped animations missing from the inventory. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-055 — Full-motion regression check.** Verifies: AC-102, AC-108. Check: with `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, load the primary pages and confirm intended animations still run and essential indicators (progress, loading) still animate; then re-check that essential motion under `reduce` contains no parallax, large-area zoom/pan, or spinning. Pass: full-motion experience intact, essential motion vestibular-safe in both modes. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- The OS setting is an instruction, not a hint.
- CSS coverage alone is not coverage — gate the JavaScript too.
- Auto-play always ships a pause; under reduced motion it never starts.
- Three flashes per second is the ceiling, in every mode.
- If removing the animation removes information, the design fails.

## Checklist

- [ ] Motion inventory lists every animation, including third-party embeds, with an assigned reduced-motion behavior (AC-104).
- [ ] Global CSS block neutralizes decorative animation and smooth scrolling under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (AC-102).
- [ ] Every JS-driven animation checks `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` and reacts to changes (AC-103).
- [ ] Emulation run passes: no non-essential animation or auto-play active under reduced motion (G-AC-051).
- [ ] Every auto-playing element has a visible pause/stop control in both modes (AC-105).
- [ ] Flash check passed on all video and animated content — never more than three flashes per second (AC-106).
- [ ] Reduced-motion task walk confirms every state change is signaled without animation and every task completes (AC-107, AC-111, G-AC-053).
